method: Single-paragraph editorial field-guide synthesis of the original 15 habitat profiles.

profiles.lowland-forest: Lowland tropical forests occur across warmer, humid plains and lower slopes, although canopy structure, vegetation and disturbance history vary with terrain, rainfall, geology and land use. A field description should distinguish mature and regenerating stands by recording canopy continuity, vertical tree layers, large stems, lianas, saplings and understory density rather than treating closed cover as proof of old growth. Slope position, drainage, nearby streams, erosion and surface soils help describe the setting, while canopy cover, tree identity where confirmed, stem measurements and disturbance evidence can make observations comparable between sites. Forest transitions are often gradual, and an elevation reading alone cannot establish a lowland forest boundary.
profiles.montane-forest: Montane forests occupy upland mountain gradients and are often cooler or wetter than nearby lowland settings, but their vegetation changes gradually with elevation, exposure and local geology. Canopy stature, changes in tree community, epiphyte abundance and understory layers are more informative in the field than a single altitude threshold. Ridge and ravine position, cloud or mist exposure, seepage and surface soils also help distinguish local conditions. Where feasible, measured vegetation height, canopy structure, temperature, humidity, slope and GPS elevation with its uncertainty provide a useful record. Submontane, montane and mossy forest boundaries differ among Philippine mountains, so their classification should follow observed vegetation and supporting evidence rather than a universal elevation band.
profiles.mossy-forest: Mossy or upper montane forest commonly has a cool, frequently wet environment, short or contorted trees and conspicuous mosses, lichens and other epiphytes, although its elevation varies with mountain climate and exposure. The amount of bryophyte cover on stems and branches, canopy stature, litter depth and epiphyte abundance help describe the formation. Mist exposure, ridge position, saturated substrates and water movement should be recorded when observed, together with temperature, humidity and measured altitude where available. Moss-covered stems, cool understory conditions and deep litter create distinctive niches for upland organisms. Disturbance and local climate can alter its structure, and a high-elevation grassland should not be classified as mossy forest merely because of its altitude.
profiles.limestone-karst: Limestone and karst forests develop across rocky terrain that may include outcrops, fissures, cliffs, pinnacles, caves and pockets of shallow soil. These features create sharply contrasting microhabitats over short distances, so the amount of exposed rock, soil depth, abrupt topography and canopy cover should be described separately. Runoff routes, dry crevices, cave moisture and cliff proximity may be relevant to a field assessment, but cave or cliff searches require their own documented effort and safe access. Plant communities respond strongly to the contrasting soil pockets and exposed limestone surfaces. The rock type must be verified rather than inferred from vegetation, and wildlife observations should retain their actual microhabitat and search context.
profiles.ultramafic-forest: Ultramafic or ultrabasic forests occur where vegetation grows on soils derived from ultramafic rock, and their plant communities can differ markedly from those on neighboring substrates. A useful field account records visible rock exposure, vegetation height and cover, leaf characteristics, patchiness and changes at the boundary with other soils. Drainage, bare-rock patches, soil color and disturbance can be noted directly, but chemical identification of ultramafic soil requires a reliable geological or laboratory source. Plant composition and structure can reflect the unusual properties of ultramafic substrates. Short trees or sparse vegetation do not, by themselves, establish an ultramafic habitat classification.
profiles.mangrove: Mangrove forests and tidal woodlands occur in intertidal or brackish coastal settings, including sheltered mudflats, estuaries and tidal river channels. Their woody vegetation may include recognizable mangrove genera such as Rhizophora, Avicennia and Bruguiera, alongside roots adapted to waterlogged, saline or periodically flooded ground. Field descriptions should distinguish tidal zones and note observed prop roots, pneumatophores, sediment, water level, inundation stage and any measured salinity. Root networks and tidal channels offer shelter and feeding areas for a variety of coastal organisms. Natural and planted stands should be distinguished, and neither a photograph nor the presence of mangrove-like plants is sufficient to establish exact salinity or an unverified plant identification.
profiles.freshwater-wetland: Freshwater marshes and wetlands are landscapes with seasonally or persistently saturated soils, standing water or slow-moving water, and vegetation ranging from emergent plants to sedge and grass communities. Their appearance varies with wet and dry seasons, so open-water patches, water-edge transitions, dominant plant growth forms and evidence of flooding should be recorded at the time of observation. Where possible, water depth, flow, clarity, conductivity, salinity and substrate can help distinguish local conditions. Aquatic vegetation and changing water edges offer a range of shelter and feeding opportunities for wetland wildlife. A single visit cannot establish whether flooding is permanent, and temporarily dry ground does not necessarily indicate that the wetland has disappeared.
profiles.riparian: Riparian forests and stream margins follow river and stream corridors where flowing water, floods and local moisture influence the vegetation and banks. Such margins can occur within lowland, montane or disturbed landscapes rather than forming an entirely separate vegetation belt. In the field, the channel, banks, flood marks, erosion, canopy and transition to adjacent vegetation help define the setting, while survey observations should distinguish in-channel, bank-edge and nearby forest positions. Stream width, wetted width, flow, depth, bed material, water temperature and distance from the bank can provide useful context when measured. Streamside vegetation, exposed banks and channel pools create a range of microhabitats for amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
profiles.disturbed-secondary: Secondary forest and disturbed mosaics include vegetation recovering after logging, cultivation, fire, storms and other disturbances, with structure that varies markedly among sites and stages of regeneration. Descriptions should consider canopy development, young trees, native and planted vegetation, gaps, stumps, invasive plants, road or trail edges and surrounding land use. Exposed soil, erosion, altered drainage, channels and evidence of recent fire can further characterize the area. Naturally regenerating and planted trees may occur together, producing a variable canopy and understory. The timing and type of disturbance, canopy and regeneration measurements, human activity and distance to habitat edges should be recorded where the evidence allows.
profiles.tropical-subalpine: Tropical subalpine rainforest is a high-elevation forest formation recognized separately from lower montane forest in the Philippine national classification. Its identification depends on the observed plant community and structure, including tree and shrub stature, canopy patches, exposure and transitions into surrounding vegetation, rather than altitude alone. Ridge position, rock exposure, drainage, slope, wind exposure and the surface organic layer can be relevant field observations. Vegetation height, canopy closure, identified dominant plants and measured temperature or humidity help document local conditions, with GPS height reported together with its uncertainty. The formation's vegetation boundaries vary among mountains and islands with the local climate and exposure.
profiles.beach-forest: Beach forest or coastal strand woodland occupies landward coastal ground above usual tidal inundation and is distinct from intertidal mangrove woodland. Its woody vegetation may grow on sand, shingle or shell-rich substrates exposed to salt spray, shoreline change and human activity. A field description should locate the vegetation relative to the active shore and record its canopy, tree stature, substrate, erosion, tourism or plantation history and natural regeneration. Tree species should be named only when identified, since plant composition differs with island, exposure and disturbance. Natural coastal woodland is not equivalent to a planted coconut belt, and tide-washed mangrove mud should not be classified as beach forest. Site history and vegetation evidence remain essential to interpreting the formation.
profiles.freshwater-swamp-forest: Freshwater swamp forest is a waterlogged forest formation distinguished from open marsh by its woody canopy and from mangrove woodland by its freshwater setting. Standing water, saturated soils, water-level marks and roots exposed to periodic inundation help characterize local conditions. Field records should consider the source and seasonality of freshwater, possible tidal mixing, drainage channels and whether the substrate is mineral or organic. Canopy cover, dominant woody plants, epiphytes, water depth and water chemistry help describe the habitat. A flooded plantation, an open marsh or a saltwater mangrove is not automatically freshwater swamp forest, and one seasonal visit may not describe its full flood regime.
profiles.peat-swamp-forest: Peat swamp forest is a forested, waterlogged formation in which accumulated organic material forms a peat substrate, unlike freshwater swamp forest developed on mineral soils. Its identification depends on evidence of organic soil layers rather than dark water or a black surface alone. The depth and condition of peat, water table, drainage, vegetation structure and signs of drying, burning or disturbance may be recorded when sampling is permitted. Woody vegetation and organic soils create distinctive patterns of drainage, root growth and regeneration. Shallow organic topsoil over mineral material must be distinguished from peat, so a soil or geological assessment is necessary before assigning the formation confidently.
profiles.semi-evergreen-rainforest: Tropical semi-evergreen rainforest is recognized as a Philippine forest formation distinct from predominantly evergreen lowland rainforest and tropical moist deciduous forest. Its description depends on the mixture of evergreen and seasonally leaf-shedding canopy components, together with tree composition, vertical structure and observations made at an identifiable time of year. Drainage, soil and local seasonal conditions should be documented where evidence is available, rather than assuming rainfall or drought from a vegetation snapshot. Confirmed tree identifications and repeated canopy observations can help distinguish natural leaf phenology from temporary damage. Loss of foliage during one visit may reflect disturbance, pests or a short dry period, so repeated or historical vegetation evidence is needed before treating a stand as semi-evergreen forest.
profiles.moist-deciduous-forest: Tropical moist deciduous forest is a seasonally leaf-shedding forest formation included in the Philippine national overview of forest types. Its identification requires attention to natural canopy phenology, mature stand structure and the balance of deciduous and evergreen tree components, rather than a dry appearance during one visit. Soil, drainage, landform, season and disturbance history help describe local conditions, while field measurements of tree community, canopy cover and understory structure make comparisons more useful. Repeated observations across seasons or published formation criteria may be needed to distinguish the natural forest type from a recently cleared, pest-affected or otherwise defoliated stand.
